old: An old English name for this plant, 'smallage,' quietly lost the naming contest to a foreign newcomer.
Its name traveled from a Greek word through Latin and a Lombard plural before landing in French.
The French called it céleri, echoing the Greek sélīnon that started it all.
clues: This garden vegetable had to fight for its place in English, eventually pushing out two older names for the very same plant, march and smallage.
Its pale green, ribbed stalks are crunchy and watery, a staple of soups and stock alongside onion and carrot. Unlike rhubarb, it is eaten savory rather than tart.
Fill its stalk with peanut butter and dot it with raisins for the snack called ants on a log, or stand one upright in a Bloody Mary.
